It is very difficult to obtain an idea of the nature of the altered zone in the vicinity 
of a fault plane.  The main source of evidence is the examination of outcrops which 
exhibit faulting.  More recently core material, taken when a deviated well crosses 
a fault, has been analysed.  The main conclusion of such studies is that there exists 
two main mechanisms of alteration and these are illustrated in Figure 43.  The first 
is termed clay smearing and corresponds to ductile clay minerals from shale streaks 
being dispersed or plastered along the fault plane during tectonic movement.  The 
extent of this phenomenon is related to the frequency and thickness of shale layers in 
the original formation.  Obviously a partial displacement of a thick clean sand will 
not exhibit permeability impairment along the fault plane  because of this effect.  The 
second mechanism which has been identified is a process of localised cementation 
in the fault region e.g. precipitation of calcite or silica.
                      
Suppose that tectonic movement has created a fracture through which preferential 
movement of formation water occurs.  The transport of precipitating ions to this
Suppose that tectonic movement has created a fracture through which preferential 
movement of formation water occurs.  The transport of precipitating ions to this site 
will result in accelerated cementation and gradually the fault zone loses permeability. 
This phenomenon is often observed in outcrops.  By the same token the growth of 
authegenic clay can also take place along the fault.
